title: Dunhuang
hook: a sealed cave library in China, holding a printed Diamond Sutra that carries its own date

segments.voice: Yesterday: Bamiyan, where two Buddhas stood in a cliff and two hollows remember them. Your line: the empty niches.

A caretaker is clearing sand from a cave temple at the edge of the desert in western China. Along one painted passage, he notices a crack in the wall. Behind it, the plaster is hollow. He breaks through and finds a small room packed floor to ceiling with scrolls, bundles, banners and paintings, sealed in and forgotten a long time, dry as the desert kept them. Among them, rolled up, is a printed copy of the Diamond Sutra.
screen: `A CAVE TEMPLE IN THE DESERT.` → `A CRACK, A HOLLOW WALL.` → `A ROOM FULL OF SCROLLS.`

segments.voice: Dunhuang was an oasis town where the roads from China met the roads west, part of the same web of old roads that ran past Bamiyan. Near it, Buddhists cut cave after cave into a cliff, the Mogao caves, and painted them floor to ceiling with Buddhas, bodhisattvas, and stories from the sutras. Why the room was sealed, nobody knows for certain. Some suggest a storeroom for worn-out texts too holy to throw away; others, a hiding place from danger. The sources are silent. What is certain is what it held: writings in Chinese, Tibetan, Sanskrit and other languages, Buddhist and not. Then the scroll: a printed Diamond Sutra, made by carving whole pages into wooden blocks, inking them, and pressing paper onto them. It opens with a picture of the Buddha teaching. At its end, a short line says who made it and why: a man named Wang Jie had it made, on behalf of his two parents, to be given away freely. Then it gives the day, the month and the year, by the Chinese calendar of the time. That line is why the British Library, which keeps it now, calls it the earliest dated printed book. Other printing may be older. But this one tells us when. How it left Dunhuang is part of the story too: explorers carried large parts of the library away, to Europe and beyond, and people still argue over whether that was rescue or taking. A son, honoring his parents, wanted the teaching to travel. It's still traveling.
screen: `AN OASIS ON THE OLD ROADS.` · `A ROOM SEALED, NO ONE KNOWS WHY.` · `WANG JIE, FOR HIS TWO PARENTS.` · `IT TELLS US WHEN.` · then, large: `THE OLDEST PRINTED BOOK.`

segments.voice: Picture a page someone made long ago so that someone else could read it, and let the breath slow. Think of the hands that carved it, inked it, carried it, kept it. You're one of the readers they were hoping for.
Dunhuang. The oasis where a sealed cave held a printed Diamond Sutra, made by Wang Jie for his parents, with its own date at the end.
Your line: the oldest printed book. One small line at its end told us when. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Copying, printing and giving away sutras has long been a way Buddhists make merit, often dedicated to parents or loved ones, as Wang Jie did; the Diamond Sutra is still chanted and studied, especially in East Asian Buddhism.

Scholars proved no printing anywhere is older than this one scroll.
